## Problem

Let $X_k \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Exp}(1)$, so $\mathbb{P}(X_k > x) = e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 0$. Define
$$\xi_n = \max_{1\le k\le n} X_k, \qquad \eta_n = \frac{\xi_n}{\ln n}.$$
We claim
$$\boxed{\eta_n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{a.s.}} 1.}$$

---

## Proof

We establish almost sure convergence (which implies convergence in probability). Fix $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$.

**Distribution of the maximum.** By independence,
$$\mathbb{P}(\xi_n \le x) = \mathbb{P}(X_1\le x,\dots,X_n\le x) = \bigl(1 - e^{-x}\bigr)^n, \qquad x\ge 0. \tag{1}$$

### Upper bound: $\limsup \eta_n \le 1$ a.s.

Take the subsequence $n_k = \lceil e^{k}\rceil$, $k\ge 1$. Using (1) and the union bound,
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\xi_{n_k} > (1+\varepsilon)\ln n_k\bigr) = 1 - \bigl(1 - n_k^{-(1+\varepsilon)}\bigr)^{n_k} \le n_k\cdot n_k^{-(1+\varepsilon)} = n_k^{-\varepsilon}.$$
Since $n_k \ge e^{k-1}$, we have $n_k^{-\varepsilon} \le e^{-(k-1)\varepsilon}$, and therefore
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}\bigl(\xi_{n_k} > (1+\varepsilon)\ln n_k\bigr) \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} e^{-(k-1)\varepsilon} < \infty.$$
By the Borel–Cantelli lemma, with probability one there exists $K(\omega)$ such that for all $k\ge K$,
$$\xi_{n_k} \le (1+\varepsilon)\ln n_k. \tag{2}$$

For arbitrary $n$ with $n_k \le n < n_{k+1}$, monotonicity of $\xi_n$ and (2) give
$$\xi_n \le \xi_{n_{k+1}} \le (1+\varepsilon)\ln n_{k+1}.$$
Since $n_{k+1}/n_k \to e$, we have $\ln n_{k+1} = \ln n_k + O(1)$, and because $\ln n_k \to \infty$,
$$\frac{\ln n_{k+1}}{\ln n} \le \frac{\ln n_{k+1}}{\ln n_k} \xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{} 1.$$
Hence, for all large $n$,
$$\eta_n = \frac{\xi_n}{\ln n} \le (1+\varepsilon)\cdot\frac{\ln n_{k+1}}{\ln n} \le (1+\varepsilon)(1+\varepsilon) = (1+\varepsilon)^2 \quad\text{a.s.}$$
(adjusting $\varepsilon$ in the intermediate step). Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ along a countable sequence,
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \eta_n \le 1 \quad\text{a.s.} \tag{3}$$

### Lower bound: $\liminf \eta_n \ge 1$ a.s.

Using (1) and the inequality $1-u \le e^{-u}$,
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\xi_n \le (1-\varepsilon)\ln n\bigr) = \bigl(1 - n^{-(1-\varepsilon)}\bigr)^n \le \exp\!\bigl(-n\cdot n^{-(1-\varepsilon)}\bigr) = \exp\!\bigl(-n^{\varepsilon}\bigr).$$
For all sufficiently large $n$, $n^{\varepsilon} \ge 2\ln n$, so
$$\mathbb{P}\bigl(\xi_n \le (1-\varepsilon)\ln n\bigr) \le e^{-2\ln n} = n^{-2}.$$
Thus
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}\bigl(\xi_n \le (1-\varepsilon)\ln n\bigr) < \infty.$$
By Borel–Cantelli, with probability one there exists $N(\omega)$ such that for all $n\ge N$,
$$\xi_n > (1-\varepsilon)\ln n, \qquad\text{i.e.,}\qquad \eta_n > 1-\varepsilon.$$
Therefore
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} \eta_n \ge 1-\varepsilon \quad\text{a.s.}$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ along a countable sequence,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} \eta_n \ge 1 \quad\text{a.s.} \tag{4}$$

### Conclusion

Combining (3) and (4),
$$1 \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \eta_n \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} \eta_n \le 1 \quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\eta_n \to 1$ almost surely (and hence also in probability and in distribution).

**Remark.** The centered statistic $\xi_n - \ln n$ converges in distribution to the standard Gumbel law $\Lambda$ with $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\le x)=e^{-e^{-x}}$, since for fixed $c\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$\mathbb{P}(\xi_n \le \ln n + c) = \bigl(1 - e^{-c}/n\bigr)^n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} e^{-e^{-c}}.$$
This confirms that $\ln n$ is the correct centering (and hence $\ln n$ the correct scaling for $\eta_n$), with the limit $1$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
